newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Egyptian envoy in Israel ahead of summit.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian envoy in Israel ahead of summit.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's envoy returned to Israel on Sunday to pave the way for a summit in Egypt with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on the crisis in Middle East peacemaking.
Egypt's embassy in Israel said envoy Osama el-Baz was in the country to meet President Ezer Weizman and Netanyahu's advisers. Israeli radio stations said he might also meet Netanyahu.

On Saturday, Israel reaffirmed it would keep building a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem, cementing its stand ahead of the summit between Netanyahu and Mubarak set for Tuesday at Egypt's Sharm el-Sheikh Red Sea resort.

Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth daily said on Sunday the summit was in danger of being cancelled because of Israel's refusal to agree ahead of time to stop building the settlement which plunged Palestinian-Israeli peacemaking into deep crisis.
A Netanyahu aide denied the report.
"We expect the summit to take place at exactly the time to which it was assigned on Tuesday, and we hope it will conclude successfully," aide David Bar-Illan told Reuters.

Netanyahu's office refused to comment on a report by Britain's Sunday Times that Netanyahu sought the summit with Mubarak after Israeli intelligence warned him of a danger of war with Arab states if settlement building continued.
Palestinians were pessimistic that Egypt, which became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel in a 1979 treaty, would succeed in reviving peace negotiations.
"We are not optimistic...because of Israel's refusal to halt settlement activities," Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo told Reuters.

"Egypt understands our position very well and it will not fall victim to Israel's tricks of promising to slow down settlement activities while on the ground it would continue to build the infrastructure of Jabal Abu Ghneim," Abed Rabbo said, referring to the settlement building in East Jerusalem.

Abed Rabbo slammed the U.S. approach to getting peace talks back on track. Palestinians want Washington to pressure Israel to stop settlement. Washington has said the sides have to make tough decisions to revive negotiations.
"As far as the U.S. is concerned, its position is disgraceful," Abed Rabbo said.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat later told reporters in Gaza he hoped the summit would succeed, calling the peace process a vital Palestinian interest.
"Despite all the obstacles (the) peace process is our strategic target and we have to do all our best to save it and to protect it," Arafat said.

On Saturday Netanyahu aide Danny Naveh said Israel would not stop building the East Jerusalem settlement. He was reacting to an Israel Television report that Israel would offer to suspend work once basic infrastructure was completed and press ahead with building homes for Arabs in East Jerusalem.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and annexed it. It says it will never cede any part of the city.

Palestinians want East Jerusalem as capital of a future state. They view settlement building as pre-empting final peace talks at which the city's fate is to be negotiated. They refuse to resume talks as long as construction continues.

Bar-Illan said the goal of the summit was to revive peacemaking but he emphasised that Israel would not stop settlement building and would stick to its demand the Palestinian Authority do more to curb "terrorism".

"The real message is that we want to resume talks with the Palestinians...but it is quite clear that our insistence on action against terrorism and violence must be the first item on the agenda," Bar-Illan said.
